query: For a CoCrFeNi high-entropy-alloy matrix evaluated in sliding from room temperature to 800 °C, what single intervention could overcome the difficulty of maintaining low coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range? Earlier studies of other self-lubricating material systems reported low coefficients of friction at 704 °C and favorable friction and wear behavior over broad temperature ranges. However, these results do not resolve the limited understanding of wide-temperature tribological performance in CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloys, and effectiveness must be maintained as operating temperature, load, and environment vary. Formulate one hypothesis that identifies a single intervention without presupposing its class, explains its mechanism, predicts friction and wear relative to the starting CoCrFeNi material, defines its temperature, load, and environmental boundaries, relates it to prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Doping CoCrFeNi high-entropy alloy with 10 at. % copper using powder metallurgy will reduce the coefficient of friction and wear rate throughout the full temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C.
generation.intervention: Doping with 10 at. % copper using powder metallurgy
generation.conditions: Temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, load of 2 N, and environment of sliding contact
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a homogeneous solid solution with a fine-grained structure
generation.mechanism: The copper doping enhances the formation of a self-lubricating CuO oxide film at elevated temperatures, reducing friction and wear
generation.predicted_outcome: Reduced coefficient of friction and wear rate compared to the undoped CoCrFeNi alloy
generation.boundary: Temperature range from room temperature to 800 °C, load up to 2 N, and environment of sliding contact
generation.uncertainty: The exact mechanism of copper doping on the tribological properties of CoCrFeNi alloy is not fully understood and requires further investigation

falsification_experiment.design: Tribological tests using a pin-on-disk scheme with a load of 2 N and a linear speed of 5 cm/s
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the coefficient of friction and wear rate of the doped CoCrFeNi alloy are not reduced compared to the undoped alloy, the hypothesis is falsified

This class of materials includes alloys consisting of at least five components with their concentrations ranging from 5 to 35 at. %. A distinctive feature of HEAs is that a thermodynamically stable substitutional solid solution with the initial fcc, bcc, or hcp lattice [] is formed due to the high entropy of mixing (>1.5 R []). This approach allows us to design new alloys with excellent combination of strength, ductility, hardness and wear resistance [,]. The presence of a high concentration of uniformly distributed passive oxide-forming elements such as Cr ensures outstanding corrosion resistance []. These features of HEAs provide their superiority over traditional steels or iron-based alloys for multi-purpose materials [,,].
CoCrFeNi alloys are common HEAs. These HEAs are promising to be used as materials for manufacturing press molds, components of magnetic systems, catalysts, etc. []. Doping with vanadium also resulted in significant alloy reinforcement and improved wear resistance threefold compared to that of the CoCrFeNiMn HEA due to precipitation of the σ-CrV solid phase. Wear resistance and tribological properties of CoCrFeNi-based HEAs can also be improved by doping them with ductile metals such as copper [,,,,]. It seems to be a promising candidate for improving the CoCrFeNi-based HEA because its physical and chemical properties are similar to those of the matrix. Nevertheless, the available data on mechanical and tribological properties of CoCrCuFeNi-based HEAs are controversial and fail to provide an unambiguous answer to the question whether copper doping is beneficial. Mechanical alloying of powder mixtures followed by hot pressing or spark plasma sintering allows obtaining materials with fine structure and uniform distribution of the elements, despite the limitations or even complete absence of their mutual solubility. This study aimed to investigate the effect of copper on the microstructure, mechanical, tribological, and corrosion properties of CoCrCuxFeNi HEAs fabricated by powder metallurgy, which involved high-energy mechanical alloying of element mixtures followed by solid-phase hot pressing. This technology allows one to produce homogeneous poreless materials from single-phase supersaturated solid solutions. This fact makes these fine-grained alloys differ from cast coarse-grained alloys with a dendritic structure. This type of structure is undesirable if high-level mechanical properties, corrosion and wear resistance need to be achieved.
